However, certain superstitious people and sons of this age, wishing to heap errors upon errors, try to defend themselves beyond the intellect and intention of <term>Scotus</term> <gloss>John Duns Scotus, a Scholastic theologian</gloss> and the canonists with these arguments: Because natural things have certain occult virtues whose cause cannot be assigned by man, such as the magnet drawing iron, and many others that <term>Augustine</term> enumerates in book twenty-one of *The City of God*. Therefore, they argue, in matters of health, where exorcisms and natural medicines fail, it should not be illicit if one sees fit to use them. But they would go further, wishing to procure health for themselves or others through images that are not <term>necromantic</term> <gloss>involving divination by the dead</gloss> or <term>astrological</term>, or through rings and such things.

Likewise, they argue: Just as natural bodies are subject to celestial bodies, so also artificial bodies, such as images, acquire certain occult virtues stemming from the influence of celestial bodies. Therefore, artificial bodies also acquire some occult virtues from celestial bodies to cause certain effects, and therefore using them and other things of this kind is not illicit. Furthermore, demons can transmute bodies in many ways, as <term>Augustine</term> says in book three of *On the Trinity*, and this is evident in the bewitched. Therefore, it is permitted to use even their power to remove those [effects].

But in truth, the statements of all holy doctors are to the contrary, and this has been made clear scattered here and there. Wherefore, regarding the first point, he says that if natural things are applied simply to produce certain effects for which they are thought to have a natural virtue, it is not illicit. If, however, they add either characters or any other unknown things and vain observations that clearly do not possess natural efficacy, this will be superstitious and illicit, as <term>Thomas</term> <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> discusses in the *Summa Theologica*, second part of the second part, question ninety-six, article two, at the end of the question.

<summary>This passage addresses the arguments used by those seeking superstitious or magical remedies for illness, refuting the claim that natural occult virtues or celestial influences justify the use of illicit images or rituals.</summary>
<keywords>superstition, occult virtues, celestial bodies, necromancy, Thomas Aquinas, Saint Augustine, bewitchment, illicit remedies</keywords>
